prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice atomic clocks, which opened the regime of fractional frequency uncertainty near 1e-18

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks rest on a specific, original idea (trapping many atoms at a magic wavelength so that the lattice does not shift the clock transition) and on its realisation with strontium. Together they moved timekeeping from the microwave caesium standard to uncertainties near 1e-18. The consequences are tangible: laboratory tests of constant drift and of relativistic time dilation over millimetre height differences, a route to redefining the second, and clock networks for geodesy. Several independent laboratories operate such clocks and compare them routinely, so the interpretation and the performance are not in doubt. The credited pair maps onto two distinct, identifiable contributions, the concept and first demonstrations (Katori) and the push to record accuracy, stability and many-body control (Ye). That keeps the prize at two names and leaves room under the three-person limit.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is overlap with prizes already given. The 2005 prize covered the frequency comb and the 2012 prize covered control of single trapped ions, and an ion-clock partisan could argue that the best clocks are not uniquely lattice clocks. There is also a fair worry that a precision-measurement prize rewards a refinement of an existing field more than a discovery. Priority details for the magic-wavelength proposal rest on my recollection, not on documents in this record. Finally, B009 has far broader opening support than any other candidate (seven of eight members rank it, two first places), and a prize to a candidate backed by three members and two first places should not be mistaken for the committee's centre of gravity.

responses.point: Danielsson ranked topological insulators first and placed optical lattice clocks sixth, citing overlap with the frequency-comb and ion-clock recognition and noting that others such as Lemonde or Lisdat might have claims.
responses.response: I take the overlap point seriously but I do not think it holds up. The comb transferred optical frequencies to the microwave domain, and the 2012 prize honoured manipulation of single quantum systems. Neither involved interrogating thousands of neutral atoms in a lattice with the light shift engineered away, which is what gives the stability and the 1e-18 accuracy. That is a separate and still-growing achievement. The Lemonde and Lisdat contributions matter for clock comparisons and fountains, but they sit downstream of the magic-wavelength idea, so I do not think they upset a two-person credit.

responses.point: Kroll ranked B026 first as the clearest case of a discovery that extends what we can measure, with a natural two-name configuration, and flagged that magic-wavelength priority was recalled from memory.
responses.response: I agree on the configuration and on the maturity argument, and I share the caveat about priority. Where I would sharpen it: the case does not rest on accuracy figures alone but on the fact that independent lattice clocks now agree with each other and with ion clocks at the 1e-18 level, which is what makes a redefinition of the second a real prospect. I would also separate this from your second choice, B037. Quantum simulation is a broad platform, and I would not want it to dilute the clean metrological story in B026.

responses.point: Eriksson noted that topological insulators have a coherent Kane-Mele-Molenkamp core, but that the 3D work and the HgTe theory proposers fall outside any three-name set, and that the entry absorbs B008 and B011.
responses.response: This is the same difficulty I see in B009. The physics is among the best on the list, and I ranked it second, but the credit is genuinely contested between Mele, Hasan and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposers, and a three-person cap forces an arbitrary cut. B026 has a much cleaner credit structure. I also doubt that broad support settles that: seven members ranked B009 highly in part because it is the least objectionable common choice. I would take B009 as my first alternative if B026 stalls, but I would want the committee to say explicitly why Hasan or the BHZ proposers are left out.

responses.point: Johansson ranked circuit QED first as a foundational enabling discovery, while declaring a professional interest in the field and acknowledging that the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits is close in subject.
responses.response: I appreciate the disclosure and I agree that circuit QED is a real discovery, not just engineering; I ranked it fourth. My disagreement is about timing: a physics prize on superconducting circuits was awarded only last year, and I would rather not follow it immediately with a closely related one when fields such as precision atomic measurement have waited. I also see an unresolved attribution question between Wallraff and Schoelkopf, and the absence of Girvin from the credited names, which makes the trio less secure than the one in B026.

responses.point: Olsson ranked magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first, arguing it is a discovery with large, growing consequences and a stable core, while acknowledging the open Andrei credit question.
responses.response: The physics is striking, and I ranked it fifth, not lower. My reservation is maturity and credit. The pairing mechanism is still unresolved, the field is under ten years old, and the Andrei claim means no three names are clean. A prize for the correlated phases themselves could be justified, but I think waiting costs us little, whereas lattice clocks are already at the stage of international metrological adoption.

uncertainties: Whether the committee sees lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
Priority and credit for the magic-wavelength proposal, which I recall from memory and have not verified.
Whether other lattice-clock leaders should have been supplied as credited names; the ballot offers only two.
Whether the committee prefers the broadly supported topological insulators entry despite its unresolved credit allocation.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with the credited names of B026 is apparent from my profile. My documented collaborations are with Anne L'Huillier, the Lund attosecond group, Ursula Keller's group, Reinhold Schuch, J. Marcus Dahlstrom, Luca Argenti and Paul Indelicato, none of whom are credited on the shortlist. I work in atomic theory and so have field proximity to the atomic and optical candidates (B026, B037, B030), which I disclose as scientific closeness, not a personal tie.
